chunks: Ibrāhīm ibn Hāshim narrated that Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, may Allah be pleased with him, was a cloth merchant.

He lost his wealth and became poor, while a man owed him ten thousand dirhams. So the man sold a house of his in which he lived for ten thousand dirhams and carried the money to his door. Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr came out to him and said: “What is this?” He said: “This is your money which is due from me.” He said: “Did you inherit it?” He said: “No.” He said: “Was it gifted to you?” He said: “No.” He said: “Then is it the price of an estate that you sold?” He said: “No.” He said: “Then what is it?” He said: “I sold my house in which I live so that I may pay my debt.”
Then Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “Ḏarīḥ al-Muḥāribī narrated to me from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام that he said:”

“A man is not to be turned out from his home because of debt. Take it back, for I have no need of it. By Allah, I am indeed in need at this time of a single dirham, yet not one dirham of it will enter my possession.”

key_terms.بَزَّازًا: a cloth merchant or textile trader
key_terms.دَيْنِي: my debt; the obligation owed by the debtor
key_terms.دِرْهَمٍ: a dirham; a unit of money in the report
key_terms.مَالُكَ: your money; the debt owed to the creditor
key_terms.مَسْقَطِ رَأْسِهِ: his place of residence or home where he lives

ai.seo_question: Can a debtor be forced to sell the house he lives in in order to repay a debt?
ai.summary: This report relates the conduct of Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr when a debtor sold his own residence in order to repay what he owed. Relying on a hadith from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he refused to accept money obtained by forcing a debtor out of his dwelling, showing both a legal limit concerning debt and a high ethical standard in dealing with others.
